questions.q: Why does reading raw (unadjusted) close prices across a stock split corrupt a backtest?
options: Raw prices are always wrong and should never be used for anything
A split causes a mechanical price drop (e.g. halving on a 2-for-1) that the engine will read as a real, massive loss even though company value didn't change
Raw prices are missing timestamps
Splits only affect options, not stocks
questions.explain: A split changes the share count and price mechanically, not the company's value. An engine using raw close will see a fake crash and distort returns, moving averages, and stop-losses around the split date.

questions.q: Why might you still want the RAW (unadjusted) price, not the adjusted close, for a rule like 'buy if price drops below $50'?
options: Raw prices are always more accurate
Adjusted price series shift retroactively every time a new dividend is paid, which can create false level-based signals that have nothing to do with the market
Adjusted prices don't include volume data
There is never a reason to use raw prices
questions.explain: Adjusted prices are rescaled retroactively, so an absolute level like '$50' means something different depending on when you downloaded the data — raw prices avoid that instability for level-based logic.

questions.q: What is the risk of forward-filling a missing price during a multi-day trading halt?
options: There is no risk; forward-fill is always correct
It assumes the price stayed flat, which can hide the fact that the price actually gapped sharply on reopening
Forward-fill deletes the surrounding data
Forward-fill only works on intraday data
questions.explain: Forward-filling is a reasonable approximation for a brief gap but becomes dangerous for a longer halt, since the eventual reopening price can be very different from the pre-halt price.

questions.q: What does 'point-in-time correctness' mean for fundamentals data like earnings?
options: Data should be timestamped with the period it describes (e.g. the quarter-end date), regardless of when it was released
Data should be recorded with the date it was actually known/released to the market, not the date of the period it describes
All fundamentals data should be discarded from backtests
It only applies to intraday tick data
questions.explain: Joining a fundamental like earnings to the period it describes instead of its actual release date gives a backtest access to information before the market could have had it — a slow-moving form of look-ahead bias.

questions.q: Why is combining a US-Eastern-timestamped bar with a Europe/London-timestamped bar risky without conversion?
options: It isn't risky — timestamps are universal
Bars that appear to align on the same calendar date may actually represent different, non-simultaneous points in time, corrupting alignment and signal logic
Timezones only matter for cryptocurrency markets
It would cause a Python syntax error
questions.explain: Without converting to a common timezone (e.g. UTC), two bars that look like they occurred at the same time can actually be hours apart, breaking any cross-asset alignment or signal timing logic.
